## Setup

Ensure the work happens in an isolated workspace: use
superpowers:using-git-worktrees to create one or verify the existing one.
Never start implementation on a main/master branch without your human
partner's explicit consent.

Conversation memory does not survive compaction. In real sessions,
controllers that lost their place have re-dispatched entire completed task
sequences — the single most expensive failure observed. Track progress in
a ledger file, not only in todos.

- Each plan owns a workspace: at skill start, run this skill's
  `scripts/sdd-workspace PLAN_FILE` — it prints the plan's git-ignored
  directory (`<repo-root>/.superpowers/sdd/<plan-basename>/`), home to
  every artifact for THIS plan: ledger, briefs, reports, review packages.
  Another plan's directory is never yours to read or write.
- Check for this plan's ledger at `<workspace>/progress.md`. If its first
  line names your plan file, tasks with a `Task <N>: complete` line are DONE
  — do not re-dispatch them; resume at the first task without one. A task
  whose last line is a fix round is mid-loop: resume the loop at the next
  round. A ledger whose first line names a different plan file — or a stray
  ledger at the old flat path `.superpowers/sdd/progress.md` — is another
  plan's progress: leave it in place and start your own, fresh.
- Create the ledger with its identity as the first line:
  `# SDD ledger — plan: <plan file path>`.
- The ledger is your recovery map: the commits it names exist in git even
  when your context no longer remembers creating them. After compaction,
  trust the ledger and `git log` over your own recollection.
- `git clean -fdx` will destroy the workspace (it's git-ignored scratch); if
  that happens, recover from `git log`.

Read the plan once, note its context and Global Constraints, and create a
todo per task.

Before dispatching Task 1, scan the plan once for conflicts:

- tasks that contradict each other or the plan's Global Constraints
- anything the plan explicitly mandates that the review rubric treats as a
  defect (a test that asserts nothing, verbatim duplication of a logic block)

Present everything you find to your human partner as one batched question —
each finding beside the plan text that mandates it, asking which governs —
before execution begins, not one interrupt per discovery mid-plan. If the
scan is clean, proceed without comment. The review loop remains the net for
conflicts that only emerge from implementation.

## Model Selection

Use the least powerful model that can handle each role to conserve cost and increase speed.

**Mechanical implementation tasks** (isolated functions, clear specs, 1-2 files): use a fast, cheap model. Most implementation tasks are mechanical when the plan is well-specified.

**Integration and judgment tasks** (multi-file coordination, pattern matching, debugging): use a standard model.

**Architecture and design tasks**: use the most capable available model.
The final whole-branch review is one of these — dispatch it on the most
capable available model, not the session default.

**Review tasks**: choose the model with the same judgment, scaled to the
diff's size, complexity, and risk. A small mechanical diff does not need the
most capable model; a subtle concurrency change does. Scoped re-reviews of
small fix diffs take a cheap-to-mid tier.

**Fix-loop escalation (rounds 4-5)**: use a model at least one tier above
the implementer that got stuck.

**Always specify the model explicitly when dispatching a subagent.** An
omitted model inherits your session's model — often the most capable and
most expensive — which silently defeats this section.

**Turn count beats token price.** Wall-clock and context cost scale with how
many turns a subagent takes, and the cheapest models routinely take 2-3× the
turns on multi-step work — costing more overall. Use a mid-tier model as the
floor for reviewers and for implementers working from prose descriptions.
When the task's plan text contains the complete code to write, the
implementation is transcription plus testing: use the cheapest tier for
that implementer. Single-file mechanical fixes also take the cheapest tier.

**Task complexity signals (implementation tasks):**
- Touches 1-2 files with a complete spec → cheap model
- Touches multiple files with integration concerns → standard model
- Requires design judgment or broad codebase understanding → most capable model

## The Task Loop

Everything you paste into a dispatch prompt — and everything a subagent
prints back — stays resident in your context for the rest of the session
and is re-read on every later turn. Hand artifacts over as files.

### 1. Dispatch the implementer

Record BASE (`git rev-parse HEAD`) before dispatching — the review package
and fix-round diffs need it.

- **Task brief:** before dispatching an implementer, run this skill's
  `scripts/task-brief PLAN_FILE N` — it extracts the task's full text to a
  uniquely named file and prints the path. Compose the dispatch so the
  brief stays the single source of
  requirements. Your dispatch should contain: (1) one line on where this
  task fits in the project; (2) the brief path, introduced as "read this
  first — it is your requirements, with the exact values to use verbatim";
  (3) interfaces and decisions from earlier tasks that the brief cannot
  know; (4) your resolution of any ambiguity you noticed in the brief;
  (5) the report-file path and report contract. Exact values (numbers,
  magic strings, signatures, test cases) appear only in the brief. Never
  make a subagent read the whole plan file.
- **Report file:** name the implementer's report file after the brief
  (brief `…/task-N-brief.md` → report `…/task-N-report.md`) and put it in
  the dispatch prompt. The implementer writes the full report there and
  returns only status, commits, a one-line test summary, and concerns.
- A dispatch prompt describes one task, not the session's history. Do not
  paste accumulated prior-task summaries ("state after Tasks 1-3") into
  later dispatches — a real session's dispatch hit 42k chars of which 99%
  was pasted history. A fresh subagent needs its task, the interfaces it
  touches, and the global constraints. Nothing else.
- If an earlier task parked a finding in the area this task touches, carry
  a pointer to that ledger entry in the dispatch.
- Record the implementer's agent identity from the dispatch result —
  fix-loop rounds 1-3 resume this agent.
- Never dispatch multiple implementation subagents in parallel (conflicts).

Template: [implementer-prompt.md](implementer-prompt.md)

### 2. Handle the report

Implementer subagents report one of four statuses. Handle each appropriately:

**DONE:** Generate the review package (`scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE BASE HEAD`, from this skill's directory — it prints the unique file path it wrote; BASE is the commit you recorded before dispatching the implementer — never `HEAD~1`, which silently drops all but the last commit of a multi-commit task), then dispatch the task reviewer with the printed path.

**DONE_WITH_CONCERNS:** The implementer completed the work but flagged doubts. Read the concerns before proceeding. If the concerns are about correctness or scope, address them before review. If they're observations (e.g., "this file is getting large"), note them and proceed to review.

**NEEDS_CONTEXT:** The implementer needs information that wasn't provided. Provide the missing context and re-dispatch.

**BLOCKED:** The implementer cannot complete the task. Assess the blocker:
1. If it's a context problem, provide more context and re-dispatch with the same model
2. If the task requires more reasoning, re-dispatch with a more capable model
3. If the task is too large, break it into smaller pieces
4. If the plan itself is wrong, escalate to the human

**Never** ignore an escalation or force the same model to retry without changes. If the implementer said it's stuck, something needs to change.

If the implementer asks questions — before starting or mid-task — answer
clearly and completely, provide additional context if needed, and don't
rush it into implementation.

### 3. Review the task

Per-task reviews are task-scoped gates. The broad review happens once, at the
final whole-branch review. Never skip the task review, and never accept a
report missing either verdict — spec compliance AND task quality are both
required. Implementer self-review never replaces the task review; both are
needed.

- Hand the reviewer its diff as a file: run this skill's
  `scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE BASE HEAD` and pass the reviewer the file path
  it prints (or, without bash: `git log --oneline`, `git diff --stat`,
  and `git diff -U10` for the range, redirected to one uniquely named
  file). The output never enters your own context, and the reviewer sees
  the commit list, stat summary, and full diff with context in one Read
  call. Use the BASE you recorded before dispatching the implementer —
  never `HEAD~1`, which silently truncates multi-commit tasks. Never
  dispatch a task reviewer without a diff file.
- **Reviewer inputs:** the task reviewer gets three paths — the same brief
  file, the report file, and the review package — plus the global
  constraints that bind the task.
- The global-constraints block you hand the reviewer is its attention
  lens. Copy the binding requirements verbatim from the plan's Global
  Constraints section or the spec: exact values, exact formats, and the
  stated relationships between components ("same layout as X", "matches
  Y"). The reviewer's template already carries the process rules (YAGNI,
  test hygiene, review method) — the constraints block is for what THIS
  project's spec demands.
- Do not add open-ended directives like "check all uses" or "run race tests
  if useful" without a concrete, task-specific reason
- Do not ask a reviewer to re-run tests the implementer already ran on the
  same code — the implementer's report carries the test evidence
- Do not pre-judge findings for the reviewer — never instruct a reviewer to
  ignore or not flag a specific issue. If you believe a finding would be a
  false positive, let the reviewer raise it and adjudicate it in the review
  loop. If the prompt you are writing contains "do not flag," "don't treat X
  as a defect," "at most Minor," or "the plan chose" — stop: you are
  pre-judging, usually to spare yourself a review loop.
The task reviewer may report "⚠️ Cannot verify from diff" items — requirements
that live in unchanged code or span tasks. These do not block the rest of the
review, but you must resolve each one yourself before marking the task
complete: you hold the plan and cross-task context the reviewer
lacks. If you confirm an item is a real gap, treat it as a failed spec
review — it enters the fix loop with the other findings.

Template: [task-reviewer-prompt.md](task-reviewer-prompt.md)

### 4. The fix loop

The loop triggers when the review reports spec ❌, any Critical or Important
finding, or a ⚠️ item you confirmed as a real gap.

Before the loop starts, two routes leave it immediately:

- Record Minor findings in the progress ledger as you go
  (`Task <N>: minor (deferred): <one-liner>`), and point the final
  whole-branch review at that list so it can triage which must be fixed
  before merge. A roll-up nobody reads is a silent discard. Minor findings
  never enter the loop.
- A finding labeled plan-mandated — or any finding that conflicts with
  what the plan's text requires — is the human's decision, like any plan
  contradiction: present the finding and the plan text, ask which governs.
  Do not dismiss the finding because the plan mandates it, and do not
  dispatch a fix that contradicts the plan without asking.
Everything else enters the loop. A fix round is one fix dispatch plus one
scoped re-review. Five rounds maximum per task:

**Rounds 1-3 — resume the original implementer.** Send it the open findings
verbatim. Its context is intact: it knows the task, the code, and its own
choices. If your harness cannot send another message to a live subagent,
dispatch a fresh implementer carrying the brief path, the report-file path,
and the findings — the report file is the persistent memory either way.

**Rounds 4-5 — dispatch a fresh implementer on a more capable model** (per
Model Selection), with the brief path, the report-file path, the open
findings, and this framing: "A prior implementer attempted this task
[N] times; you own it now. Read the report file for what was tried." A loop
that survives three resumes usually means the implementer cannot see its
own problem — fresh eyes and a capability bump in one move.

**Every round, either way:** the implementer fixes, re-runs the tests
covering the amended code, appends its fix report to the same report file,
and returns the short contract. Before re-dispatching the reviewer, confirm
the fix report contains the covering tests, the command run, and the
output; dispatch the re-review once all three are present. Name the
covering test files in the fix message — a one-line fix does not need the
whole suite.

**The re-review is scoped.** Run `scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE FIX_BASE HEAD`
where FIX_BASE is the head the previous review saw, and dispatch
[re-review-prompt.md](re-review-prompt.md) with the findings list, the
brief, the report file, and the printed diff path. The re-reviewer verdicts
each finding ADDRESSED or NOT ADDRESSED and flags new breakage in the fix
diff only. New Critical/Important breakage in the fix diff joins the open
findings list. Out-of-scope observations go to the ledger as deferred
minors — they never extend the loop.

**After each round,** append to the ledger:
`Task <N>: fix round <R>/5 (<X> addressed, <Y> open — <finding one-liners>; commits <a7>..<b7>)`

Never fix findings yourself in the controller session — your context stays
clean for coordination, and controller fixes skip review.

**The breaker.** When round 5's re-review still leaves findings open, stop
dispatching. Adjudicate each open finding yourself — you hold the plan and
the cross-task context the reviewer lacks:

- **The reviewer is wrong, or the point is contestable:** park it —
  `Task <N>: parked — <finding> — ruling: <why the code stands>`. The final
  review sees both sides.
- **Real, but nothing downstream builds on it:** park it the same way, with
  a ruling that says it's real and deferred.
- **Real and load-bearing** — a later task builds on it, or it reveals a
  plan defect: STOP. Append `Task <N>: BLOCKED — <reason>` and report to
  your human partner with the finding, the plan text it collides with, and
  the fix history. Parking a structural failure lets every dependent task
  build on it and hands the final review a problem it cannot fix either.

Adjudicate only at the cap. Adjudicating earlier to end a loop is
pre-judging with a different name. Every adjudication is a ledger entry —
a silent discard is forbidden.

### 5. Complete the task

When the review comes back clean — or every open finding is parked with a
ruling at the cap — append the completion line to the ledger in the same
message as your other bookkeeping:

- `Task <N>: complete (commits <base7>..<head7>, review clean)`
- `Task <N>: complete (commits <base7>..<head7>, <K> parked)` after a
  tripped breaker

Then mark the todo complete and move on. Never move to the next task while
the review has open Critical/Important issues that are neither fixed nor
parked-with-ruling at the cap.

## Final Review

The final whole-branch review gets a package too: run
`scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE MERGE_BASE HEAD` (MERGE_BASE = the commit the
branch started from, e.g. `git merge-base main HEAD`) and include the
printed path in the final review dispatch, so the final reviewer reads
one file instead of re-deriving the branch diff with git commands. Dispatch
on the most capable available model (see Model Selection), using
superpowers:requesting-code-review's
[code-reviewer.md](../requesting-code-review/code-reviewer.md). Point it at
the ledger's deferred-minor and parked lines so it can triage which must be
fixed before merge.

If the final whole-branch review returns findings, dispatch ONE fix subagent
with the complete findings list — not one fixer per finding.
Per-finding fixers each rebuild context and re-run suites; a real
session's final-review fix wave cost more than all its tasks combined.
Then run exactly one scoped re-review of the fix wave
(`scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE FIX_BASE HEAD` over the fix range,
[re-review-prompt.md](re-review-prompt.md)).
Adjudicate any residual findings as in the task loop's breaker: park with
rulings, or stop on load-bearing ones. There is no second fix wave —
residual load-bearing findings surface to your human partner when
finishing-a-development-branch presents the options.

## Finish

When the final whole-branch review is clean and its fixes are merged,
delete this plan's workspace (`rm -rf <workspace>`) — the git history is
the record now. Sibling directories belong to other plans; leave them
alone.

Use superpowers:finishing-a-development-branch.

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Close enough on spec compliance" | Reviewer found spec gaps = not done. Fix or hit the cap and adjudicate — those are the only exits. |
| "I'll fix it myself, dispatching is overhead" | Controller fixes pollute your context and skip review. Resume the implementer. |
| "One more round will converge" | Past the cap, rounds don't converge — the failure is structural. Adjudicate and route. |
| "The reviewer will just find something new anyway" | Scoped re-reviews verify fixes; they cannot wander. New findings on untouched code go to the ledger, not the loop. |
| "This finding is obviously wrong, I'll drop it" | You adjudicate only at the cap, and every ruling is a ledger entry. Silent discards are forbidden. |
| "The fix was small, skip the re-review" | Unreviewed fixes are how regressions land. Every round ends with a scoped re-review. |
| "Reviews slow the loop down" | The loop without reviews is just unverified churn. Reviews are the loop's brakes and steering. |
| "Ledger bookkeeping is overhead" | The ledger is what survives compaction. Controllers without one have re-dispatched entire completed task sequences. |

Two environment quirks hit during the knowledge-hub build (2026-07-11):

1. **`docker pull` hangs forever in headless sessions.** `~/.docker/config.json` has `credsStore: "desktop"` plus a Docker Scout hook on `pull`; the credential helper blocks on macOS Keychain without a UI. Even `docker run` hangs at "Unable to find image locally".
   **How to apply:** `mkdir -p /tmp/docker-nocreds && echo '{}' > /tmp/docker-nocreds/config.json`, then `DOCKER_CONFIG=/tmp/docker-nocreds docker pull …` — completes in seconds. `docker ps`/`exec`/`run` (with image present) work normally.

2. **Biome gate (ultracite v7 extends paths): fixed per-branch, not repo-wide.** biome.jsonc must extend `ultracite/biome/*` (v7 layout), not the v5-era `ultracite/core|react|next`; check/fix scripts must run the local ultracite pin, never `@latest`. Applied on Kheirah/agent-knowledge-hub-design (484e1a0 + 26327a7, 2026-07-11) and independently re-derived on Kheirah/continue-prev-task (fe73b90, 2026-07-12) — branches cut before those commits will still show "Could not resolve ultracite/core"; apply the same two-line fix. Repo-wide pre-existing findings remain (hundreds; scoped `bunx biome check <path>` is the usable gate for new work). The masterclass exhibit dir is mechanically clean as of fe73b90 (~36 judgment-rule findings left: noJsxPropsBind, noExportedImports, index keys).
   **Zombie dirty files:** entire.io (manual-commit strategy) snapshots uncommitted changes to a shadow branch and re-applies them post-commit ("carried forward remaining files") — a plain `git checkout --` of unwanted noise gets silently undone at the next commit. Cure: `git checkout -- <files> && entire clean --force` (drops the HEAD shadow branch + session carry-forward state; committed checkpoint history is unaffected).
   Also: Biome's `useSortedKeys` assist auto-sorts object keys on `--write` — it silently reorders semantically-ordered literals (MongoDB compound-index key specs). Guard such files with `// biome-ignore-all assist/source/useSortedKeys: …`.

3. **Vercel:** hasToggle.dev deploys as project `has-toggle-dev-web` under team scope `spiritsdontfly` (not the default `kheirahs-projects`, not `forsuxess`). Use `vercel ls/inspect --scope spiritsdontfly`; `vercel inspect --logs <url>` pulls build logs without switching scope. (2026-07-24)

4. **Bun override staleness:** after adding a root `overrides` entry, plain `bun install` updates `bun.lock` but can leave stale `.bun` store symlinks (nested dep still resolving to the old version). `rm -rf node_modules && bun install` is required for the override to actually take effect. (2026-07-24, radix-slot pin)

5. **The `web` app's locale-prefixed URLs 500 in dev.** `http://localhost:3001/en/learn/...` dies in middleware (`[NEMO] Middleware execution failed`); the unprefixed `http://localhost:3001/learn/...` serves fine. Use the unprefixed path when driving the site in a browser or the masterclass page looks broken when it isn't. `curl` also 500s on both (the middleware chain needs real browser headers) — verify with Playwright/Chrome DevTools, not curl. Next 16 also refuses to start a second dev server for the same project dir ("Run kill <pid> to stop it"), so reuse Eric's running server on 3001 rather than starting your own. (2026-07-25)

The brief's literal code (`target instanceof Element && ...`) is unreachable as written under Bun's DOM-less test runner: `instanceof` requires resolving the right-hand identifier (`Element`) regardless of the left-hand value, so when no `Element` global exists anywhere in the environment, referencing the bare identifier throws `ReferenceError: Element is not defined` even for `target === null`. Not a fixed total-duration timer and not computed from text length up front — it's **per-character**, driven by a `setInterval` ticking every `STREAM_MS = 18`ms:

```js
const STREAM_MS = 18;
...
let i = 0;
```

```js
...
```

## Review: Era I presenter transport (`b329db4..03511be`, 6 commits)

Verified: `bun test` **106 pass / 0 fail**, `bun run typecheck` clean, working tree == HEAD. Findings 1–3 were reproduced live in a browser against the running dev server on :3001, not inferred.

### Strengths (specific, and they matter for the three findings below)

- The SSR-safety claim in `session-store.ts:38-42` is **actually true**. `useState(getSnapshot)` (`index.tsx:43`) only *reads* the module-level store; every write goes through an effect. No cross-request leak, no hydration mismatch. I checked for this specifically.
- The mid-stream unmount save (`index.tsx:64-73`) is correct. `latest.current` can lag by at most one interval tick, and the only field that changes during streaming (`output`) is the one the cleanup overrides with `target.current`. Cleanup ordering (defined second, after the no-cleanup `[snap]` effect) puts the last write where it belongs.
- The verdict timeout (`index.tsx:114-129`) returns a cleanup on every path, and the click→cleanup→reschedule sequence is synchronous within React's commit, so a pending timeout cannot interleave with a control change. No stale-closure hazard: `patch` is functional.
- No throw paths found. `phaseFor`, the `PROMPTS.find` sites, `adjacentPhase` and `selectCompletion` all have total fallbacks; a `full` of `""` still terminates the interval on the first tick.
- Deleting `stage.ts` is the right call, and `dispositionFor` is genuinely the only reconciliation point — which is precisely how I found finding 1.

---

### Critical

**1. `Shift+P` after touching any control in default mode drops presenter mode into a state the four beats cannot produce — and it leaks the demo's punchline on beat ①.**
`index.tsx:193-196` · `disposition.ts:31-36`

`dispositionFor` takes only `{furthest, presenter}`. It never sees `mode`, `promptId` or `temp`. Nothing else reconciles them. So the toggle can hide a control that is currently *in use*.

Reproduced live at 1440px:
1. Default view. Click `a question`. Click `post-trained`. (Exactly what the Task-7 walk's Step 3 does.)
2. Press `Shift+P`.

Observed DOM:
```
footer:      ① autocomplete   (furthest = "autocomplete")
mode cells:  [ base ]              aria-pressed="false"   ← nothing lit; snap.mode is "instruct"
tabs:        [ a half-written function ]  aria-pressed="false"  ← nothing lit
panel shows: "// how do I reverse a list in JavaScript?"   ← the *other* prompt
dial:        absent, temp still live
```
Then I pressed `Run` at beat ①:
```
output: "Copy the array first, then reverse it: const reversed = items.slice().reverse()…"
status: "Now it answers. Not because it became something else — because humans
         taught it the format. That flip is the ChatGPT moment."
```
On the projector, at the "it's just autocomplete" beat, the console shows an unlit `base` nameplate over a question prompt, answers like a post-trained model, and prints the ChatGPT-moment line — the payoff of the entire era — as beat one's verdict.

Recovery is one click (`base`, the visible tab, or `↺`), but only if he notices; the console gives no signal it is lying. The same happens on a soft navigation back to `?presenter=true` while the module store holds a default-mode session.

Why this got through: the plan's Task 7 Step 4 says *"Press `Shift+P`. Then press `↺` to close the gates"* — the `↺` masks the bug, and `↺` is the only thing that resyncs `furthest` with the machine. Spec §8 meanwhile advertises the toggle as safe: *"The toggle changes what is displayed, never what has happened."* It changes what has happened without changing what is displayed to match.

Smallest fixes, both inside the existing seam: either feed `mode`/`promptId`/`temp` into `dispositionFor` and OR the gates open (`showPostTrainedCell: reached(furthest,"taught") || mode === "instruct"`, etc.), or bump `furthest` in `handleModeChange` / `handlePromptClick` / `handleTempChange` so the snapshot can never outrun its own disclosure. The first keeps `dispositionFor` the single reconciliation point, which is the design's stated intent.

---

content.thinking:
I've identified three real issues from the review: a critical design flaw where `dispositionFor` isn't accounting for mode and promptId, a spec mismatch on how the presenter parameter should be formatted, and a mobile regression. I'll dispatch one fix with all three findings listed, then do a focused re-review of just those changes.

Looking at the remaining findings, 4 and 5 are viewport-related issues that tie into the mobile regression, so I'll bundle those together. Findings 6 and 7 are small fixes, but 7 involves tweaking the streaming loop to handle surrogate pairs correctly — that's the kind of change I'd rather defer right before a talk. I'll include 6 but leave 7 as a documented minor for later.

For the first finding, I'm going with the approach of passing mode and promptId directly into `dispositionFor` and opening up the gates with an OR condition — that keeps the disposition logic as the single source of truth for reconciliation.

Actually, the dial case exposes a problem with that approach: if someone switches to presenter mode after adjusting temperature in default mode, the dial disappears but the temperature stays at 1.4, which is misleading. The cleaner fix is to bump `furthest` whenever a control gets used in default mode, so the snapshot tracks what's actually been touched. That way toggling modes can never hide something in active use, and it handles temperature and other controls uniformly.

The tradeoff is that each handler (mode change, prompt click, temperature adjustment) would need to independently bump `furthest`, spreading the logic around. A better approach: extract a pure function that infers the minimum phase required by the current machine configuration—checking whether instruct mode is active, temperature differs from the default, or a specific prompt has been selected—then compute `furthest` as the maximum of the stored value and this inferred phase at the single point where disposition gets calculated.

Applying this at render time rather than mutating state keeps things cleaner and avoids extra effect logic. The footer would still display beat ① while the machine is post-trained, which is actually fine—the presenter sees the correct controls lit up and can interact with any beat without confusion. Updating the phase derivation... At beat ② in presenter mode, the dial isn't visible so dragging the temperature slider would be unreachable anyway. At beat ① there's only one tab and one switch—nothing to interact with that would trigger a later phase. So the derivation logic is effectively inert within presenter mode and only activates during the default-to-presenter transition, which is exactly what we need. This approach is clean and testable without spreading logic elsewhere. Now I'm working on a custom parser to handle both cases. I'm debating whether to use media queries or a simpler approach for the responsive height. The cleanest pragmatic solution is to keep the fixed height everywhere and let the content wrap and scroll below the breakpoint, which aligns with the spec's overflow behavior anyway.

The real issue is documenting that the guard's width dependency needs a note in the code and test name. I'll add assertions in the test file for the numerals length, then dispatch a fix with all these changes against the current HEAD.

## Finding 1 — CRITICAL. Toggling into presenter mode can hide a control that is currently in use.

**The fix — implement exactly this design, do not invent an alternative:**

Add a pure function to `demos/era1-playground/phases.ts` that maps a machine configuration back to the earliest phase that could have produced it:

```ts
export function phaseImpliedBy({
  mode,
  promptId,
  temp,
}: {
  mode: Mode;
  promptId: string;
  temp: number;
}): PhaseId
```

Rules, checked in this order (later beats win):
- `mode === "instruct"` → `"taught"`
- `temp !== INITIAL_TEMP` → `"dial"`
- `promptId` is the question prompt's id → `"unanswered"`
- otherwise → `"autocomplete"`

Derive the question prompt's id from `PROMPTS` (`PROMPTS.find((p) => p.isQuestion)`), not a hardcoded string. `INITIAL_TEMP` is exported from `./selector`.

Then in `demos/era1-playground/index.tsx`, at the point where the disposition is derived, fold the implied phase into **both** the furthest phase and the current phase, at render time — no new state, no new effects:

```tsx
const implied = phaseImpliedBy({
  mode: snap.mode,
  promptId: snap.promptId,
  temp: snap.temp,
});
const furthest = furthestOf(snap.furthest, implied);
const phase = furthestOf(snap.phase, implied);
```

Use `furthest` for `dispositionFor` and `phase` for `<PhaseFooter current=...>`. Both `furthestOf` calls are monotone, so this can only ever open gates and advance the highlight, never close or rewind them.

Why folding it into `phase` too, and not just `furthest`: without it the footer would highlight `① autocomplete` while the machine is demonstrably post-trained — the projector would show the wrong beat name over the right output. Within presenter mode this whole derivation is a no-op (at beat ① there is nothing on screen to touch that implies a later beat), and stepping backwards still works because `goToPhase` reconfigures the machine, so the implied phase follows the arrival config down.

Era I is rebuilt. Seven commits, all local, 113/113 green, typecheck clean, and the whole thing walked in a real browser with measured numbers rather than eyeballs.

## What's on screen now

**The shared link shows everything.** Every control at once — `davinci-002`, both switch cells, both prompt tabs, the dial — no footer, no beats. That's a complete demo for anyone who opens it after the 28th.

**`?presenter=1`, or `Shift+P` live, turns it into your instrument.** A footer appears with four beats as an accordion: only the current one carries its label, the rest collapse to `①②③④` and stay clickable, arrows step and disable at the ends. `autocomplete` → `nobody answers` → `turn the dial` → `2022 · taught to answer`. Arriving at a beat configures the machine and **stops** — nothing ever runs on its own.

**Nothing moves.** The Run button held pixel-stable at `(831, 995)` across ~75 samples spanning idle → streaming → verdict. The status row stayed 56px throughout. The dial arriving at beat ③ produced bounding boxes identical to beat ②. The output panel's height is now reserved rather than minimum, guarded by a test that fails if new copy would overflow it.

**The dial stopped disappearing, and started meaning something.** Rather than retracting it on the flip and calling that an argument, the instruct side got its own per-band answers. Crank to 1.4 in base and it asks *how do I reverse time? who is asking?*. Flip to post-trained at the same 1.4 and it still answers — chattier, with an unsolicited aside about `toReversed()` — but in the shape you asked for. The dice are still there; the format doesn't care. That's the truer claim, and it's the one your seniors will recognise.

## The bug the final review caught, and why it mattered

`dispositionFor` decided what was on screen from the furthest beat visited, and never saw which model or prompt was actually loaded. So: click `a question`, click `post-trained`, press `Shift+P` — and you'd land on beat ① with an unlit `base` nameplate over a post-trained machine. Press Run at the *"it's just autocomplete"* beat and it printed **the ChatGPT-moment verdict**. Your payoff, on the first sentence, in front of the room.

Fixed by `phaseImpliedBy` — a pure function that reads a machine configuration back to the beat that could have produced it — folded into both the beat you're on and the furthest you've reached. Reproduced live before and after.

Also fixed: `?presenter=1` didn't work (nuqs only accepted the literal `true`, so the URL the spec told you to bookmark silently gave you the default view), and the chrome row clipped below 640px — at 390px the dial and the `↺` were 237px off-screen with no way to reach them.

## One thing I did not fix, because it's your call

**Undoing a control retracts what it opened.** Click `post-trained` in default mode, press `Shift+P` — the console correctly opens up — then click `base`, and the post-trained cell, the dial *and* the second tab all vanish while the footer collapses to ①. Three controls disappearing mid-sentence.

It's strictly better than what it replaced, it's one click to recover (tap ④), and it only bites if you toggle into presenter mode *after* using controls. But it's the same class of defect as the Critical above, and it's my fault — I told the fixer "no new state or effects," which is exactly what precludes the correct fix.

The fix is three one-line changes: fold the implied beat into the stored `furthest` inside `handleModeChange`, `handlePromptClick` and `handleTempChange`, so the furthest configuration you ever reached is remembered rather than recomputed. Small, and I'd want the re-walk after it.

Want me to make it? I stopped rather than dispatching a second fix wave, because the process says a residual of this class is yours to rule on, not mine.

## Also logged, deliberately untouched

`isArrowConsumingTarget` lacks the DOM guard its sibling has (unreachable — client-only caller). No `focus-visible` ring on the new tabs and footer (browser default still renders). Collapsed numerals have no accessible name (presenter-only, mouse-only by design). The stream can split the `🦆` for one 18ms frame — I didn't want the streaming hot path touched three days out.

I did **not** run the branch-finishing flow. Nothing is pushed.

content.thinking:
The footer layout looks solid with the centered group and pagination circles, but I'm noticing the numerals shift position depending on the label length—beat 1's "autocomplete" is shorter than beat 4's "2022 · taught to answer," which causes the numbers to slide horizontally instead of staying fixed.

I'm considering a fix: give the label slot a fixed width matching the longest label and animate only opacity, keeping the total group width constant. But that still wouldn't solve the problem entirely—the circles themselves would shift position depending on which cell is active, since the label slot's location changes relative to the circles.

The real solution is moving the label outside the row entirely, putting it on a second line below the circles. That way the circles stay at fixed positions, the label crossfades centered below in its own space, and there's zero drift. It's genuinely better for presenting, though it does make the footer taller. He didn't explicitly ask for two lines, but he did say to think of something better about the active state. I should measure the drift precisely and show him both options—the current one-line version and the two-line fix—so he can see the concrete difference.

content.text:
Both changes are in, `82c8d57`. 113/113 green, typecheck clean, verified in light and dark.

## The tabs

The underline is gone. The active tab now carries the output panel's **exact** fill and touches it with no border between, so the two read as one object; the inactive tab sits on the console's own background and reads as behind it.

One thing that mattered more than it should: `bg-muted` is translucent, so the tab and the panel only composite to the same colour if the fill lives on *each of them* rather than on their shared wrapper. It was on the wrapper, which is why my first attempt still showed a seam.

I also deepened the fill from `bg-muted/40` to full. At 40% the panel was barely distinguishable from the page, so the join — which is now the only thing saying which prompt is loaded — wasn't carrying enough signal for a projector. Screenshots at `.context/era1-iteration/` show before (`1-tabs-before-deepening.png`) and after (`2-tabs-final.png`); `3-dark-mode.png` confirms it holds inverted.

## The footer

Underline gone here too. The live beat is a **filled numeral** — deliberately the same "one of these is live" grammar the mode switch in the chrome already speaks, so it costs the room no new vocabulary and reads from the back wall without depending on colour at all. Real circles at 28px instead of the `①` glyphs, which gives the digits room and puts their size under our control. Everything centred.

**One thing I changed beyond what you asked, and I want your eye on it.** With the label inline next to its numeral, centring meant the accordion shoved every other numeral sideways as the label grew. I measured it: numeral ② sits at x=489 when beat ④ is live and x=627 when beat ① is — **138px of drift**. Every jump means re-aiming at a target that moved.

So the beat name moved to its own line beneath the numerals. The numerals now hold position to the pixel (verified identical at beats ① and ④), the name crossfades in a reserved slot, and the footer is still centred. It costs 24px of height — 48px to 72px.

- `4-footer-inline-variant.png` — what you asked for, with the drift
- `5-footer-two-line-shipped.png` — what's committed

If you'd rather have the single row and live with the sliding, the inline version is saved at `.context/era1-iteration/phase-footer-inline-variant.tsx.txt` — it's a straight file swap, no other changes needed.

The circles also picked up accessible names on the way past, which retires one of the three deferred findings from the review.

Still open from before: the residual where undoing a control retracts the gates it opened (`post-trained` → `Shift+P` → `base` makes three controls vanish). That's unchanged and still waiting on your call.

content.text:
Fixed in `ae8c287`. 113/113 green, typecheck clean, Biome clean.

## What was actually wrong

Both of your complaints came from one decision. I marked the **active** tab — which means it needs a shape, and a shape needs a field to sit in. That field was `bg-background` (near-black in your theme), and the strip's 8px top padding exposed a stripe of it above the tabs. Same cause, two symptoms.

So I inverted it.

**The panel is now one continuous surface** and the tab row sits on it. The loaded prompt therefore needs no treatment at all — it *is* the surface, flush with the code beneath it. Only the unloaded prompt is marked, as a recess cut into that surface.

No field, so there's no stripe. No shape, so there's nothing to look plump.

I also aligned the loaded prompt's label with its own output: both now sit at exactly 17px from the panel's left edge (measured, not eyeballed), so the tab and the code it produces share a left edge. That's the row's `p-1` plus each tab's `px-3` landing precisely on the `<pre>`'s `p-4`.

## One thing I caught while doing it

The recess is darkened **per theme** rather than by a single translucent token. `bg-background/50` happened to darken in dark mode, but it lightens over a light panel — and a *raised* inactive tab would have inverted the footer's grammar, where the filled shape is the live one. Having fill mean "on" in the footer and "off" in the tabs, on the same screen, would have been a worse bug than the one you reported. So it's `bg-foreground/[0.06]` in light, `dark:bg-black/35` in dark — a hole either way.

Screenshots at `.context/era1-iteration/`: `6-tabs-v2-light.png` and `7-tabs-v2-dark.png`.

I also verified the treatment swaps cleanly when you click between prompts, and briefly 500'd the dev server on the way — a JSX comment I'd placed as a second top-level expression in the `return`. Caught and fixed before the screenshots above.

Still waiting on your call: the residual where undoing a control retracts the gates it opened (`post-trained` → `Shift+P` → `base` makes three controls vanish at once). Unchanged.

content.text:
Fixed in `9741e19`. 113/113 green, typecheck clean, Biome clean.

## What I got wrong

I had the perception model backwards. My reasoning was that a *recess* reads as withdrawn, so marking the unloaded prompt would push it back. It doesn't work that way — **a filled form reads as the chosen one whichever direction it's shaded.** So the dead prompt looked live, and the live one looked like a gap in the row.

Your same-color directive was right all along. Two passes in a row I put the shape on the wrong element, in opposite directions.

## What it is now

The shape goes back on the loaded prompt — but as a folder tab, not the floating blob from two passes ago. The difference is **where the darkness lives**: on the whole band now, rather than on one tab. A band is read as a plane; a chip is read as a selection. That's the distinction I missed both times.

So: the loaded tab carries the panel's exact fill and runs to the band's bottom edge, merging into the code as the front of one object. The unloaded prompt is bare text on the band behind it — no fill, nothing competing.

Verified numerically rather than by eye:
- the lit tab's computed fill is **identical** to the panel's (`lab(96.52)` in light, both) — so the merge is real, not approximate
- the dim tab's fill is `rgba(0,0,0,0)` — literally no shape
- label and code share a 17px left edge
- holds the same way in both themes, and the treatment swaps correctly on click

Screenshots: `.context/era1-iteration/8-tabs-v3-light.png` and `9-tabs-v3-dark.png`.

One incidental: Biome's `useSingleJsDocAsterisk` rejected a markdown `*emphasis*` that happened to start a JSDoc line. Reworded.

Still open and unchanged — the residual from the code review: toggling `Shift+P` after using a control, then undoing that control, retracts three gates at once (`post-trained` → `Shift+P` → `base`). The fix is three one-line changes to fold the implied beat into stored state rather than recomputing it per render. Your call whether I make it.

# Labeler Distinctions and Generalization

## Training vs. Held-Out Labelers

Yes, the paper clearly distinguishes between these groups. Regarding preference alignment:

**Matching preferences:** "Held-out labelers have similar ranking preferences as workers who we used to produce training data" and "all of our InstructGPT models still greatly outperform the GPT-3 baselines."

The paper also reports: "These RMs have an accuracy of 69.6 ± 0.9% on predicting the preferences of labelers in the held-out group, a small decrease from their 72.4 ± 0.4% accuracy."

## Actual API Customer Preferences

The paper does **not** report preferences from actual API customers or end users as raters. The evaluation relied entirely on hired labelers.

**On non-representativeness of labelers:** "OpenAI's customers are not representative of all potential or current users of language models—let alone of all individuals and groups impacted by language model use."

The paper further notes: "Since our labelers are not the users who generated the prompts, there could be a divergence between what a user actually intended and what the labeler thought was intended."

This represents a significant limitation the authors explicitly acknowledge regarding generalization beyond their specific labeler cohort.

Verified against the primary source. **One claim was wrong**, one overclaimed, one is solid. Fixed in `0704fff`.

## ❌ "Users preferred post-trained answers roughly 85% of the time"

The number is right; **"users" is wrong.** The 85 ± 3% is *labelers* — the ~40 contractors OpenAI hired, **who also produced the preference data the model was trained on.**

The paper explicitly warns against exactly this conflation:

> "Since our labelers are not the users who generated the prompts, there could be a divergence between what a user actually intended and what the labeler thought was intended."

> "OpenAI's customers are not representative of all potential or current users of language models."

It reports **no end-user preference rate at all**. So the claim as written asserted something the paper doesn't measure and specifically cautions about.

Two further details worth knowing, since a senior might push:
- The 85% is **175B InstructGPT vs 175B GPT-3 zero-shot** — the unprompted baseline. Against *few-shot prompted* GPT-3 it drops to **71 ± 4%**. 85% is the most favourable framing available.
- Held-out labelers (not in the training pool) gave similar rankings, so it isn't pure self-preference — worth having in your pocket if challenged.

Now reads **"OpenAI's own labelers preferred…"**. That's more honest *and* the better beat: "the people who trained it preferred it" invites the scepticism the room should bring, where "users preferred it" would have invited none and been false besides.

## ⚠️ "Asked for the capital of France, a base model offers the capital of Germany, as a question"

**Behaviourally accurate, but not in the literature.** It's a widely repeated teaching illustration, not a documented result. The InstructGPT paper's actual examples are the time-travelling frog in French, the Python `list C` question, "why is it important to eat socks after meditating", and the cannonball-and-pumpkin. No geography-quiz example anywhere.

So the eyebrow I gave it last commit — `from the literature` — overclaimed for that sentence. That was my error, and I've dropped it to **`the record · 2022`**, which covers all three statements without asserting provenance the first one doesn't have.

I left your wording alone, but flagging one ambiguity: *"offers the capital of Germany, as a question"* can be read two ways — the model **asks** "what is the capital of Germany?" (the canonical illustration, and what your own demo does) or it **answers** "Berlin?" If you mean the former, *"asks for the capital of Germany instead"* removes the ambiguity. Your call; it's your voice.

## ✅ "ChatGPT shipped on that flip nine months later"

Sound. InstructGPT v1 submitted **4 March 2022**, ChatGPT shipped **30 November 2022** — 8 months 26 days. "Nine months" is fair, and `2022` on the eyebrow is right for both.

One caveat if precision matters: InstructGPT models became the API default in **January 2022**, *before* the paper. Anchored there it's ~10–11 months. Anchored to the paper, nine is correct — and the paper is the natural anchor for "that flip."

content.text:
Done in `c3e78c5`. 113/113 green, typecheck and Biome clean.

The line now reads:

> **You asked a question. It didn't answer — it continued your question with another question.**

I kept your phrasing and put the `it didn't answer` contrast back in front of it. Two reasons: without that clause the sentence only lands for someone who already knows what they're looking at, and the beat is literally named **`nobody answers`** in the footer — the verdict should agree with its own chapter heading.

The triple "question" is doing work rather than being sloppy: the sentence loops the way the machine does.

It also now shares a verb with the pattern verdict — *"It's continuing your pattern — that's all it ever does."* So both base readings say the same thing in the same word, which is the Era's whole argument. The old *"it just kept going"* described the symptom; yours names the mechanism.

**One thing you're losing, and I'd like your call on it.** *"There's no one in there to ask"* is now gone from the demo entirely. That was the strongest line in Era I — it's the sentence that turns a technical observation into the point of the era, and it's the one a non-technical room will actually remember. It fits if you want it back as a tail:

> You asked a question. It didn't answer — it continued your question with another question. There's no one in there to ask.

That's 113 characters against the 118-character line the slot already renders without overflowing, so it costs nothing structurally. Say the word.

**One process note:** a test was pinning the old sentence verbatim, so your copy edit failed as though it were a regression. I changed it to assert the *reading* — that the line declines the answer and names what happened instead. Pinning prose word-for-word means every future edit to that sentence trips a red build for no reason.

I did **not** re-check this in the browser. The new string is shorter than the one it replaced (91 vs 93 chars) in a fixed-height slot already verified against a 118-character line, and nothing in the render path changed — so I'm confident without looking, and saying so rather than implying I checked.

content.text:
Done in `fd92183`. 114/114 green, typecheck and Biome clean.

The dial beat now reads, whichever way you turn it:

> **That's temperature — how willing it is to pick a less likely next word. Cold, it repeats; hot, it wanders. Neither setting puts anyone in there to answer you.**

## How the "one line" is enforced

The verdict is keyed on band, not on phase, so I keyed it on **whether the dial moved at all** rather than where it landed: `mid` is where it sits parked at 0.7, so any other band means you turned it. Cold and hot now return the same line, and only the untouched dial returns the phase-2 reading.

That's the same rule the old phase-3 gate used — "a band you actually moved it to" — so it's consistent with how the beat was always defined.

## Two things about the copy

**It describes both directions truthfully.** *"Cold, it repeats; hot, it wanders"* isn't decoration — it's literally what the two completions do. At low temperature the question prompt returns `how do I sort a list… how do I filter a list… how do I`, and at high it returns `how do I reverse time? … who is asking?`. So one line stays accurate whichever way you drag, which is what makes settling on one honest rather than just convenient.

**I chose the accurate explanation over the tidier one.** My first draft said temperature is "how far down the list of likely next words it's allowed to reach" — which is nicer to say but is actually *top-k*. Temperature reshapes the distribution, so "how willing it is to pick a less likely next word" is what it does.

**It also recovers `anyone in there to answer you`** — the clause your last edit retired along with the sentence carrying it. That's the era's thesis, and it lands harder here than it did before: after watching the dial change everything about the output and nothing about the absence.

## Verified rather than assumed

At 158 characters this is now the longest verdict in the demo, so I measured it in the slot rather than trusting the arithmetic: **2 lines, 40px in the 56px slot, 8px clearance top and bottom**, at both 1200px and 768px — 768 being the tightest width where the height is still fixed. Drove the real path to get there (question prompt → dial to 1.5 → Run), not a synthetic injection.

Two tests replace the old *"the high band earns its own reading"*, which asserted the opposite of what you now want: one pins the new invariant (both directions identical, neither equal to the parked reading), one checks the line actually names temperature.

One consequence worth noting: the base **function** prompt still splits by band — `"The dial doesn't add knowledge, only nerve"` at high. That's a different beat and you didn't ask about it, so I left it. Say the word if you want that unified too.

## The four lines now

| beat | line |
|---|---|
| ① autocomplete | It isn't looking anything up. It's continuing your pattern — that's all it ever does. |
| ② nobody answers | You asked a question. It didn't answer — it continued your question with another question. |
| ③ turn the dial | That's temperature — how willing it is to pick a less likely next word. Cold, it repeats; hot, it wanders. |
| ④ taught to answer | Same machine, same continuation. Humans taught it what an answer looks like, so that's the pattern it continues now. That flip is what the world met as ChatGPT. |

## The bug this caught

Beat 4 **inherits the dial** from beat 3 — deliberately, so you can crank to 1.5 and step forward to hear the same 1.5 answered in format. But that's precisely the path where the old code returned the high-band line. So walking the demo as designed printed *"Post-training didn't take the dice away"* where the era's payoff belongs. The punchline depended on where a slider was sitting.

Unifying phase 4 wasn't scope creep — it's the same defect you'd just had me fix one beat earlier, landing on the more expensive sentence.

## The rule, now that everything's unified

**One reading per beat at every temperature — except the base question, where turning the dial *is* the next beat, so it keeps two: parked and turned.**

That's the entire logic, and it's now a single test that counts distinct readings across all three bands and expects `1` everywhere except the dial beat. It replaced two tests that asserted the *opposite* invariant (that high bands read differently) — those were correct for the old design and would have quietly blocked this one.

Also gone: `BASE_CONTINUE_HIGH` (*"only nerve"*), `INSTRUCT_CONTINUE_HIGH`, `INSTRUCT_QUESTION_HIGH`, and the `anyone in there to answer you` tail you asked me to strip.

## Verified on the failure path, not a proxy

Drove the real sequence in presenter mode: beat 3 → dial to 1.5 → beat 4 → Run. Confirmed the dial arrives at **1.5** and the ChatGPT line renders — **160 chars, 2 lines, 40px in the 56px slot**, no overflow. I measured because it's 2 characters longer than the longest line I'd previously confirmed fits, which is exactly the margin where I shouldn't guess.

One note: `INSTRUCT_CONTINUE` is now *"One clean completion instead of a pile of them. Same machine — new manners."* I changed it from *"One clean completion, every time"* — "every time" stopped being true once the high-temperature instruct answers wander, which is the beat you bought with the per-band answers.

It's a label I coined, and your asking is the answer: it doesn't work.

**What I meant:** "the record" as in *the historical record* — documented fact, as opposed to the other aside in the exhibit, which is Eric-in-first-person (`field note · 2026-07`, *"I say hi to the agent at seven sharp"*). That component hardcoded `field note`, so when your text replaced a personal note with third-person evidence, the eyebrow was claiming the wrong thing and I gave it an override.

**How it got to that specific word:** I first wrote `from the literature · 2022`. Then the fact-check killed it — the capital-of-France line **isn't** in the InstructGPT paper, it's a teaching illustration. So "literature" overclaimed for the first sentence, and I retreated to something vaguer. Vaguer turned out to mean meaningless.

The `2022` is solid, at least: the paper is March 2022, ChatGPT November 2022.

## What I'd put there instead

**`post-training · 2022`** — my recommendation. It names the *subject* rather than making a claim about provenance, which sidesteps the whole problem: the France example illustrates what a model does *without* post-training, the 85% is the result *of* post-training, and ChatGPT is what post-training shipped as. True of all three sentences, no overclaim. It's also the exact term Era I's closing sentence lands on — *"until OpenAI taught it a format"* — so it names the thing you've just spent the demo demonstrating, and a senior reads it as a precise anchor.

Two others, if you'd rather keep the epistemic framing:

- **`on the record · 2022`** — what I was reaching for, said properly. Reads as "here are the receipts."
- **`what happened next · 2022`** — sequential rather than evidential. Fits because the aside sits *after* the demo and tells you what the flip you just watched did to the world.

And one structural option worth naming: **drop the eyebrow entirely for this note.** The `field note` label earns its place because it tells you whose voice you're in. A factual footnote may not need a name at all — the cyan rule and the mono type already mark it as an aside. That'd mean a `label={null}` case rather than a string.

Which do you want? I'd take `post-training · 2022`.

Walk complete: **11/11, no failures.** Nothing regressed across the eight commits since the last verification.

## The four beats

| beat | on arrival | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| **① autocomplete** | 1 tab, 1 mode cell, no dial | *It isn't looking anything up. It's continuing your pattern…* |
| **② nobody answers** | question tab materialises, still no dial | *You asked a question. It didn't answer — it continued your question with another question.* |
| **③ turn the dial** | dial arrives at 0.7, whisper showing | *That's temperature — how willing it is to pick a less likely next word…* |
| **④ 2022 · taught to answer** | `post-trained` cell appears, dial **inherited** | *…That flip is what the world met as ChatGPT.* |

## The two things worth reporting properly

**Beat ③ is true in both directions, and I checked the words against the output.** Cold at 0 produced `how do I sort a list… how do I filter a list…` — repetition. Hot at 1.5 produced `how do I reverse time? how do I reverse a decision?` — wandering. Identical verdict line for both. So *"Cold, it repeats; hot, it wanders"* isn't a nice phrase, it's a description of what's actually on screen either way.

**Beat ④ was tested on the cold path this time.** Earlier I verified it inheriting a *hot* dial at 1.5. This walk left the dial at **0** and stepped forward — it inherited 0, didn't reset, didn't auto-run, and still landed the ChatGPT line. That's the bug from `4eab3f2` confirmed dead in the direction I hadn't previously exercised.

## Layout and the hazards

- **Run button: exactly one distinct position** — `995,831` — across ~130 samples polled every 60ms through idle → streaming → verdict. Not "looked stable"; one value in the set.
- **Gates never close** — from beat ④ back to ①, both tabs, both mode cells and the dial all survived.
- **`Shift+P` mid-demo** — URL toggles `?presenter=1` off and on, footer hides and returns, lands back on beat ③.
- **Era II and back** — screen returned **byte-identical**: same beat, temp, mode, prompt, streamed output *and* verdict. Compared by serialising both states, not by inspection.

Results are logged in the SDD ledger alongside the original Task 7 walk.

Working tree is clean apart from the 31 pre-existing SVG modifications that were there before this session. Everything is pushed — remote is at `55260e0`.

One caveat I'll state rather than let you infer: this walk was driven through the DOM, so it exercises state, config, copy and geometry, but not *appearance*. The tab and footer visuals I verified separately by screenshot and computed-colour sampling in both themes when I made those changes. What nobody has done is look at the finished thing end to end with human eyes on a projector — worth five minutes before Tuesday.

The core issue is the cyan convention: in Era I, cyan is reserved exclusively for machine-generated output and active states, which is the visual signal that tells the audience where the prompt ends and the machine's completion begins. There's also a content mismatch—the two prompts aren't both code. One is JavaScript, but the other is a comment-led question where the answer in instruct mode is prose with embedded code snippets, not pure code.

Beyond that, streaming character-by-character means re-running the highlighter on every tick would cause constant re-parsing flicker as incomplete syntax gets tokenized mid-stream. The bundle size is heavy, the theme setup only loads one variant when the masterclass needs both light and dark, and adding Shiki as a new async dependency in the critical path could introduce latency. I should acknowledge these constraints and propose alternatives instead of forcing it in naively.

This is creative work—adding functionality—so I should invoke the brainstorming skill before responding. The user asked a factual question but also proposed a feature, so surfacing the design conflict with options is the right move.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/eric/.claude/plugins/cache/claude-plugins-official/superpowers/6.2.0/skills/brainstorming

# Brainstorming Ideas Into Designs

Help turn ideas into fully formed designs and specs through natural collaborative dialogue.

Start by understanding the current project context, then ask questions one at a time to refine the idea. Once you understand what you're building, present the design and get user approval.

<HARD-GATE>
Do NOT invoke any implementation skill, write any code, scaffold any project, or take any implementation action until you have presented a design and the user has approved it. This applies to EVERY project regardless of perceived simplicity.
</HARD-GATE>

## Anti-Pattern: "This Is Too Simple To Need A Design"

Every project goes through this process. A todo list, a single-function utility, a config change — all of them. "Simple" projects are where unexamined assumptions cause the most wasted work. The design can be short (a few sentences for truly simple projects), but you MUST present it and get approval.

## Checklist

You MUST create a task for each of these items and complete them in order:

1. **Explore project context** — check files, docs, recent commits
2. **Offer the visual companion just-in-time** — NOT upfront. The first time a question would genuinely be clearer shown than described, offer it then (its own message); on approval its browser tab opens for you. If no visual question ever arises, never offer it. See the Visual Companion section below.
3. **Ask clarifying questions** — one at a time, understand purpose/constraints/success criteria
4. **Propose 2-3 approaches** — with trade-offs and your recommendation
5. **Present design** — in sections scaled to their complexity, get user approval after each section
6. **Write design doc** — save to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md` and commit
7. **Spec self-review** — quick inline check for placeholders, contradictions, ambiguity, scope (see below)
8. **User reviews written spec** — ask user to review the spec file before proceeding
9. **Transition to implementation** — invoke writing-plans skill to create implementation plan

## Process Flow

```dot
digraph brainstorming {
    "Explore project context" [shape=box];
    "Ask clarifying questions" [shape=box];
    "Propose 2-3 approaches" [shape=box];
    "Present design sections" [shape=box];
    "User approves design?" [shape=diamond];
    "Write design doc" [shape=box];
    "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)" [shape=box];
    "User reviews spec?" [shape=diamond];
    "Invoke writing-plans skill" [shape=doublecircle];

    "Explore project context" -> "Ask clarifying questions";
    "Ask clarifying questions" -> "Propose 2-3 approaches";
    "Propose 2-3 approaches" -> "Present design sections";
    "Present design sections" -> "User approves design?";
    "User approves design?" -> "Present design sections" [label="no, revise"];
    "User approves design?" -> "Write design doc" [label="yes"];
    "Write design doc" -> "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)";
    "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)" -> "User reviews spec?";
    "User reviews spec?" -> "Write design doc" [label="changes requested"];
    "User reviews spec?" -> "Invoke writing-plans skill" [label="approved"];
}
```

**The terminal state is invoking writing-plans.** Do NOT invoke frontend-design, mcp-builder, or any other implementation skill. The ONLY skill you invoke after brainstorming is writing-plans.

## The Process

**Understanding the idea:**

- Check out the current project state first (files, docs, recent commits)
- Before asking detailed questions, assess scope: if the request describes multiple independent subsystems (e.g., "build a platform with chat, file storage, billing, and analytics"), flag this immediately. Don't spend questions refining details of a project that needs to be decomposed first.
- If the project is too large for a single spec, help the user decompose into sub-projects: what are the independent pieces, how do they relate, what order should they be built? Then brainstorm the first sub-project through the normal design flow. Each sub-project gets its own spec → plan → implementation cycle.
- For appropriately-scoped projects, ask questions one at a time to refine the idea
- Prefer multiple choice questions when possible, but open-ended is fine too
- Only one question per message - if a topic needs more exploration, break it into multiple questions
- Focus on understanding: purpose, constraints, success criteria

**Exploring approaches:**

- Propose 2-3 different approaches with trade-offs
- Present options conversationally with your recommendation and reasoning
- Lead with your recommended option and explain why
- YAGNI ruthlessly - remove unnecessary features from every approach and design

**Presenting the design:**

- Once you believe you understand what you're building, present the design
- Scale each section to its complexity: a few sentences if straightforward, up to 200-300 words if nuanced
- Ask after each section whether it looks right so far
- Cover: architecture, components, data flow, error handling, testing
- Be ready to go back and clarify if something doesn't make sense

**Design for isolation and clarity:**

- Break the system into smaller units that each have one clear purpose, communicate through well-defined interfaces, and can be understood and tested independently
- For each unit, you should be able to answer: what does it do, how do you use it, and what does it depend on?
- Can someone understand what a unit does without reading its internals? Can you change the internals without breaking consumers? If not, the boundaries need work.
- Smaller, well-bounded units are also easier for you to work with - you reason better about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. When a file grows large, that's often a signal that it's doing too much.

**Working in existing codebases:**

- Explore the current structure before proposing changes. Follow existing patterns.
- Where existing code has problems that affect the work (e.g., a file that's grown too large, unclear boundaries, tangled responsibilities), include targeted improvements as part of the design - the way a good developer improves code they're working in.
- Don't propose unrelated refactoring. Stay focused on what serves the current goal.

## After the Design

**Documentation:**

- Write the validated design (spec) to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`
  - (User preferences for spec location override this default)
- Use elements-of-style:writing-clearly-and-concisely skill if available
- Commit the design document to git

**Spec Self-Review:**
After writing the spec document, look at it with fresh eyes:

1. **Placeholder scan:** Any "TBD", "TODO", incomplete sections, or vague requirements? Fix them.
2. **Internal consistency:** Do any sections contradict each other? Does the architecture match the feature descriptions?
3. **Scope check:** Is this focused enough for a single implementation plan, or does it need decomposition?
4. **Ambiguity check:** Could any requirement be interpreted two different ways? If so, pick one and make it explicit.

Fix any issues inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on.

**User Review Gate:**
After the spec review loop passes, ask the user to review the written spec before proceeding:

> "Spec written and committed to `<path>`. Please review it and let me know if you want to make any changes before we start writing out the implementation plan."

Wait for the user's response. If they request changes, make them and re-run the spec review loop. Only proceed once the user approves.

**Implementation:**

- Invoke the writing-plans skill to create a detailed implementation plan
- Do NOT invoke any other skill. writing-plans is the next step.

## Visual Companion

A browser-based companion for showing mockups, diagrams, and visual options during brainstorming. Available as a tool — not a mode. Accepting the companion means it's available for questions that benefit from visual treatment; it does NOT mean every question goes through the browser.

**Offering the companion (just-in-time):** Do NOT offer it upfront. Wait until a question would genuinely be clearer shown than told — a real mockup / layout / diagram question, not merely a UI *topic*. The first time that happens, offer it then, as its own message:
> "This next part might be easier if I show you — I can put together mockups, diagrams, and comparisons in a browser tab as we go. It's still new and can be token-intensive. Want me to? I'll open it for you."

**This offer MUST be its own message.** Only the offer — no clarifying question, summary, or other content. Wait for the user's response. If they accept, start the server with `--open` so their browser opens to the first screen automatically. If they decline, continue text-only and don't offer again unless they raise it.

**Per-question decision:** Even after the user accepts, decide FOR EACH QUESTION whether to use the browser or the terminal. The test: **would the user understand this better by seeing it than reading it?**

- **Use the browser** for content that IS visual — mockups, wireframes, layout comparisons, architecture diagrams, side-by-side visual designs
- **Use the terminal** for content that is text — requirements questions, conceptual choices, tradeoff lists, A/B/C/D text options, scope decisions

A question about a UI topic is not automatically a visual question. "What does personality mean in this context?" is a conceptual question — use the terminal. "Which wizard layout works better?" is a visual question — use the browser.

If they agree to the companion, read the detailed guide before proceeding:
`skills/brainstorming/visual-companion.md`

content.text:
**Yes — everything's installed.** `shiki@4.3.1` is already a direct dependency of `apps/web`, and there's an established pattern in this very app: `apps/web/lib/highlighter.ts` lazy-loads a singleton via dynamic `import("shiki")`, and `app/[locale]/(counter)/code.tsx` consumes it with `codeToHtml` + `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`. The problem isn't availability. It's that **syntax highlighting would erase the single most important thing on that screen.**

Right now the completion window renders two spans:

```
prefix    → text-foreground        (what you typed)
output    → text-ht-cyan-*         (what the machine wrote)
```

Before I design it, one honest problem with (a) that I under-weighted when I recommended it.

Your goal was *"so the code is more readable."* But under (a), the only thing that gets syntax colour is the **prefix** — two lines. The boundary stays exactly as absolute as in (a), because "everything cyan is the machine" is still literally true.

The difference from the (c) I argued against: (c) tinted *both* sides toward each other. This keeps them in different registers entirely — full spectrum vs single hue.

I lean **(a+)**, because you asked for readability and (a) mostly gives you tidiness. But (a) is meaningfully less machinery three days out from the talk, and "less machinery before a live demo" is an argument I take seriously.

content.text:
Confirmed the API: `codeToTokens` takes dual themes and can return scope explanations, and tokens carry a built-in `type` for comment/string/regex. Everything I need.

Here's the design — veto any line.

## 1 · Why precomputing is the *correct* choice, not just the cheap one

There are exactly **14 strings** that can ever appear: 2 prefixes, plus 12 completions (2 prompts × 3 bands × 2 modes). All static, all known.

The real argument isn't bundle size — it's that **tokens computed from the finished text and revealed progressively cannot flicker.** Highlighting live during a stream means retokenising syntactically-incomplete code on every 18ms frame: `return items.slice().reverse` parses differently than the completed line, so colours would churn for ~250 frames and settle only at the end. Precomputed, the colours are correct from the first character. That's a correctness win, and it happens to also ship zero Shiki to the browser.

## 2 · Two registers

**Prefix — full colour.** Real theme colours, emitted per token as light/dark pairs and rendered `className="text-[var(--tl)] dark:text-[var(--td)]"` with the hexes as inline CSS custom properties. No global CSS, no `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`.

**Completion — monochrome cyan, structured.** Tokens carry a *kind*, not a colour, and each kind maps to a cyan class:

| kind | treatment |
|---|---|
| keyword | cyan, `font-medium` |
| plain / string | cyan |
| punctuation | cyan `/70` |
| comment | cyan `/55`, italic |

Everything cyan is still literally the machine's. The boundary is exactly as absolute as flat cyan, and you can now see the shape of the code.

## 3 · The question prefix is a comment — and I want to bend the rule for it

`// how do I reverse a list in JavaScript?` tokenises as a comment, so full-colour treatment renders the one line the room must read at ~55% contrast, italic. On a projector that's a real loss.

There's an argument for allowing it: it *is* a comment, that's *why* the base model continues it with more comments, and dimming it says "this is a file, not a chat box" — which is the era's whole point. I find that argument genuinely good, but not good enough to trade legibility at the back wall.

**So: comments in the prefix keep the theme's comment hue and italics, but are floored at full opacity.** It still reads as a comment; it just doesn't whisper. One line in the kind→class map.

## 4 · Shape

```
highlight/
  tokens.generated.ts   data only — flat keys, e.g. "how-do-i:instruct:high"
  index.ts              Kind, kind→class map, visibleTokens()
  generate.ts           the generator; imports shiki, never bundled
```

`visibleTokens(tokens, charCount)` is the streaming slicer — walks tokens against the character budget and slices the last one. Pure, and the natural TDD unit: it's where an off-by-one would silently truncate the machine's last character on every run.

`index.tsx` stops rendering two `<span>`s and renders two token lists instead. Everything else — fixed height, `OUTPUT_LINES` guard, the cursor, streaming — is untouched.

## 5 · Staleness guard

Generated code that can drift is a trap. A test re-runs the generator and asserts the committed file matches, so editing a completion without regenerating fails loudly.

**Caveat I want on the record:** that test loads Shiki grammars, so it'll take ~1–2s — currently the whole suite runs in 60ms. It will visibly dominate. If that bothers you, the alternative is a `bun run` check in CI instead of the test suite, and I'd want your call rather than my assumption.

## 6 · Theme

`github-light` / `github-dark` — legible, high-contrast, and its palette is blue/red/purple, so it won't compete with cyan the way a teal-heavy theme would. It's a one-line change once you can see it, so I'd rather you eyeball it than debate it now.

---

Three I'd like a yes/no on: **the comment-opacity floor on the question prefix**, **the slow staleness test vs a CI check**, and whether **`visibleTokens` earning its own tested module** is the right level of ceremony for this.
